property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) sets owner to the supplied address x; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender, so for some fuzzed _owner values (where _owner != caller) the mutant's owner differs from the supplied _owner and thus violates the rule.

For all callers and supplied addresses, only the current owner can change the owner via setOwner (i.e., after calling setOwner via any caller, the owner is equal to the caller iff the caller was the prior owner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner restriction so some non-owner caller can change owner and break this invariant.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) leaves C.owner equal to the provided _owner (reference); the mutant that sets owner = address(0) breaks this because after setOwner it will instead be address(0) for some fuzzed _owner values.

General rule: only the current owner can successfully call setOwner; the mutant requiring msg.sender != owner breaks this by allowing non-owners to call setOwner and therefore changing owner when invoked by a non-owner.

Invariant: only the externally calling EOA that is currently stored in owner can successfully call setOwner (so after any call to setOwner by msg.sender the contract's owner becomes the provided new owner); the mutant using tx.origin instead of msg.sender allows a call relayed through a contract (where msg.sender != tx.origin) to bypass owner check and thus lets a non-owner contract cause owner to change, violating the invariant for some relayed-call inputs.

For all callers, only a direct transaction from the current owner (i.e., msg.sender == owner) can change owner via setOwner; the mutant using tx.origin allows an owner-change when the call is relayed through a contract (msg.sender != tx.origin), so a relaying contract can change owner even when msg.sender is not the original owner.

For all calls to setOwner, only an external account that is the current owner when calling (msg.sender == owner) can change owner; the mutant that uses tx.origin instead allows a relaying contract (msg.sender != tx.origin) to change owner, breaking this property for some inputs.

For every call to setOwner initiated by an EOA who is the current owner (msg.sender == owner), the owner is successfully updated; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead can be tricked by a relaying contract to change owner when msg.sender != owner, so there exist inputs (a relayer contract address and a target new owner) that make the mutant's owner differ from the reference.

Only direct calls whose msg.sender equals the current owner can change owner via setOwner; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead can be triggered by a relayer contract so that a caller whose msg.sender != owner (but tx.origin == owner) can change owner, violating the rule for some relayed-call inputs.

For every caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(...) completes and returns true in the reference; the mutant changes the return value to false for at least some inputs, breaking this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address argument, calling setOwner(...) completes and the reference contract always returns true; the mutant instead returns (previous == _owner) and thus can return false when setting to a different address, violating the rule.

For every call to setOwner by the current owner, the reference contract always returns true (indicating success); the mutant returns false when the new owner is address(0), violating this universal success-return rule for some input.

For any caller equal to the current owner and any target address _owner, calling setOwner(_owner) updates the public owner getter to _owner; the mutant that omits the assignment leaves owner unchanged for some inputs.
